title: Aperture & Depth of Field

learn.summary: Depth of field — how much of the scene is acceptably sharp — is the photographer's pointing finger. Shallow depth isolates a subject from a busy world; deep focus lets a landscape breathe front to back. Aperture is the main lever, but focus distance and focal length pull on it too.

do: Take two photos of the same person or object: one with blurred background (portrait mode or get close), one with everything sharp — decide which told the story better.

children.title: The F-Stop Scale

learn.summary: The full-stop sequence — f/1.4, 2, 2.8, 4, 5.6, 8, 11, 16, 22 — multiplies by √2 each step, halving the light every time. Most lenses are sharpest two or three stops down from wide open, often around f/5.6–f/8. Memorize the sequence; it is the times table of photography.

do: Recite the full-stop scale from f/1.4 to f/22 from memory tomorrow morning — then once more without looking at the end of the week.

children.title: Controlling Depth

learn.summary: Three levers make depth of field shallower: open the aperture, move closer to the subject, or use a longer focal length. Phones fake shallow depth computationally (portrait mode) because their tiny sensors keep nearly everything sharp — but getting physically close to a subject produces real optical blur even on a phone.

do: Shoot a cup from 3 meters, 1 meter, and 20 cm with your phone (no portrait mode) and watch the background blur grow as you close in.

children.title: Bokeh

learn.summary: Bokeh (from Japanese boke, "blur") is the aesthetic character of out-of-focus areas — how highlights render as discs, whether edges are smooth or nervous. Distant fairy lights behind a close subject are the classic bokeh test. It is a quality judgment, not a quantity: more blur is not automatically better bokeh.

do: After dark this week, focus on an object 30 cm away with city or string lights far behind it and photograph the light discs you get.
